headline: Pin map V6 is frozen and built into every head board, the end-to-end trace from each ASIC connector pin to its FPGA ball passes, and the tall capacitors under the Frontend are gone. No system blocker is left; 14 majors are. Before any head is ordered: the fabricator must confirm ten layers in 0.8 mm for the ASIC boards (R2S-03), the ASIC designer still owes the capacitor values, the bond diagram and the die height (SYS-31), and the Frontend panel puts break-off tabs on the edge 0.567 mm from the near ASIC board (SYS-57). findings.title: Unkeyed DF40 pairs let an ASIC board mate rotated 180 degrees, putting +/-8 V onto ASIC clock and data pins.
findings.what: Hirose states the DF40 connector is not polarized, and no head board has a key, hole, standoff or an orientation mark that stays visible after mating (the Frontend has no silkscreen; the LDO and ASIC boards have only pin-1 triangles, hidden under the mated connector). A rotated Frontend cannot mate in a full stack, because its bottom parts sit over the LDO J3 (Option B: J5) header and it overlaps the ASIC board or router in the same 1.5 mm plane, so it rests at least 1.6 mm high and its contacts never touch. The real exposure is ASIC boards on the LDO underside connector J4 (router J4 on Option B) and ASIC boards stacked on ASIC boards, where nothing stops a rotated fit; on LDO A J4 only about 0.1-0.3 mm of 1206 capacitor height is in the way, less than the 0.45 mm engagement. A partly built stack (a Frontend fitted before the J3 ASIC board, or the Option B LDO board without its router) is also exposed.
findings.where: ASIC board J3/J4 on FPGA-LDO A J4 (bottom), on router J4, and ASIC board on ASIC board; also LDO A J3 and Frontend J1/J2 on LDO J1/J2 in a partly built stack. Nets: LDO /ASIC_VDD10 (U9 LT3042, +10 V), /ASIC_VSS10 (U10 LT3094, -10 V), /ASIC_DVDD; ASIC board /AGND, /DGND.

findings.title: Option B cannot carry pin map V6: J5 would need at least 132 contacts, the DF40 series stops at 120, and the 5.3 mm router/LDO-board overlap has no room for a second connector.
findings.what: V6 adds 6 lines per ASIC port. J5 would then carry 120 signals plus the 9 ASIC rails and 3 returns: 132 contacts against its 120/120. Hirose makes the DF40 only up to 120 positions, and J5 is already that part, so the 'larger DF40' option in SYS-06 does not exist. findings.title: High-load stacks reach the 637 mA port current limit on a 1.8 m cable with 30-32 AWG or thinner +5 V wire.
findings.what: Each stack (Frontend, FPGA-LDO board and four ASIC boards) gets all its power through pin 19 of its Micro-HDMI cable, a single +5 V wire. The Frontend buck U16 draws close to constant power, so when the cable voltage drops its current rises. With a perfect cable the high-load case needs about 0.55-0.58 A, below the port switch's 637 mA minimum limit, but once the cable loop resistance passes about 0.9-1.3 ohm (30-32 AWG at 1.8 m) it reaches that limit, and at 34-36 AWG there is no usable operating point. The expected load works on every gauge; the Frontend power has never been estimated with Vivado/XPE and the chosen cable's wire gauge is unknown, so a power estimate and a measured cable loop resistance are needed.
findings.where: HDMI Extension Board U701-U708 (TPS2553DBVR, R711-R718 37.4k) OUT -> PORT1_5V..PORT8_5V -> J610-J617 pin 19; cable +5 V wire; Frontend J3.19 -> VIN_5V -> U16 MPM3833C (IN 13/14, EN 4) -> VIN_3V3 -> every Frontend regulator and J2.68-70 to the FPGA-LDO board (its only supply input). Load: inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md section 1 gives 1.2 W / 2.4 W at VIN_3V3, which already include 0.13 / 0.30 A for the LDO/ASIC boards (0.30 A is the DF40 contact rating, not an estimate); a review working file (not published) gives 1.45 W expected and 2.79 W high at 5 V, about 5 % above the record. The high case is a pessimistic envelope (VCCINT 0.4 A, every stimulator at full current).

findings.title: Each port's 44 chip outputs return through two DGND contacts; the far chips' lines now run beside the DGND plane but still start over AGND.
findings.what: Each 80-pin port has AGND only on pins 42/44 and DGND only on 46/48. With two real boards stacked, the 44 outputs of four chips return through the two DGND contacts at the FPGA-LDO joint, and the far board's 22 outputs also cross a second joint with the same four returns. On the far (top) board those outputs, including both returned CLK32MHZ clocks, run 4-7.5 mm on In4 between the REF_VDD plane (In3) and the VDD10/VDD_DRIVER plane (In5). Their return current reaches ground mainly through rail capacitors that go to AGND (and plane-to-plane capacitance), then leaves the stack on AGND pins 42/44 and crosses to GND at NT1 on the FPGA-LDO board, through the reference and analog ground of every chip in the port. SYS-41 asked that the second board keep clock lanes on a DGND-referenced layer; V3 does not. The six spare pins 2/4/6/8/24/58 are now nets on both V3 boards but no-connect on FPGA-LDO A and the router, so using them as extra grounds later needs an FPGA-LDO change. The files cannot show how large the effect is.

findings.title: Option B J5 carries 108 signals with only three return contacts: GND on pins 3 and 65 and AGND on pin 62.
findings.what: J5, the 120-pin DF40 board-to-board connector between the Option B router and LDO board, uses every contact: 108 single-ended 1.5 V signals, 9 ASIC rails and only three returns. A fast signal's return current flows back along the nearest ground path, and 51 of the 108 signals are more than 5 mm from a GND contact, so about 80 lines switching together at 32 MHz can cause crosstalk and ground bounce. The AGND planes on both boards also act as reference planes for signal layers, and AGND joins GND at NT1 about 6.6 mm from J5, so pin 62 carries switching digital return current as well as the analog return of eight ASICs; that mixing is the main analog risk, while the DC drop (about 1-4.4 mV) is negligible. ASIC output edge rates are not documented, so the files cannot show whether three returns are enough; a decision on more returns, or measured edge rates, would settle it.
findings.where: Option B router J5 (DF40C-120DS) and LDO board J5 (DF40C-120DP): GND pins 3 and 65, AGND pin 62; the four MP pads on the LDO-board header have no net. findings.title: If all eight stacks share one head ground electrode, as SYS-11 advises, every J1 lead becomes a supply-return path through ASIC AGND (where REF_1-4 are bonded) and NT1, carrying about 4-27 mA in a typical lead and 9-62 mA (up to 89 mA) in the most-loaded one, so load steps put up to about 13 mV on the recording reference.
findings.what: Each stack returns its whole supply current (0.15-0.55 A) through its own HDMI cable ground. The eight stack grounds therefore sit tens of mV apart, and the offsets move with each stack's load. On both V4 ASIC boards the chips' REF_1-4 pads and the one-pin J1 are on AGND, so whatever ties the animal to a stack also sets that stack's recording reference. One shared ground electrode is the usual rule for low-power headstages and is what SYS-11 proposes. Here it makes the head leads a parallel return path: part of every stack's supply current flows through J1, the ASIC AGND plane, the DF40 AGND contacts and NT1, and the voltage drop along the lead appears on every channel. Separate electrodes instead drive DC current through the tissue.
findings.where: ASIC boards V4 (both): J1 (PinHeader 1x01 at 144.875, 68.28) and U01_BCD1/2 REF_1-REF_4, LREF_GND1-4, RREF_GND1-4 on /AGND; no part ties AGND to DGND. FPGA-LDO A: NT1 (100.58, 121.0) is the only AGND-GND tie, with only 1.0 mm test pads TP5 (GND, 92.5, 144.4) and TP6 (AGND). Option B: the router, which stays on the head, has no ground pad, and its AGND reaches NT1 (LDO board, 100.58, 126.81) only through J5.62. Cable ground: J610-J617 and Frontend J3 pins 4/7/10/13/16 and shell.

findings.corrected: If all eight stacks share one head ground electrode, as SYS-11 advises, each stack's J1 lead becomes a parallel supply-return path through ASIC AGND (where REF_1-4 are bonded), the DF40 AGND contacts and NT1. findings.already_known: The rate is open per the FE schematic V46 note ('GT link rate/protocol ... unverified'); inputs/hdmi/design_inputs/START_HERE.md records 1.25 Gb/s as an assumption but is not flagged as wrong anywhere, and the eight-ASIC multiplier is missing there, so this is not known as an open item.
findings.title: Each cable's one GT lane must carry eight ASICs, but the only recorded line rate (1.25 Gb/s) counts one ASIC.
findings.what: Each Frontend sends all its recording data over one GT (multi-gigabit transceiver) lane, U1 TX0, through its HDMI cable. That lane must carry all eight ASICs on the Frontend: 64 data lines, 2.048 Gb/s raw or 1.536 Gb/s once the 12-bit words are packed. The only recorded line rate, about 1.25 Gb/s with an 800 ps bit, was worked out from one ASIC per port; after 8b/10b coding (a line code that sends 10 bits for every 8 data bits) it leaves only 1.0 Gb/s. A workable lane is 2.5 Gb/s (packed data) or 3.125 Gb/s (raw frames), and no line rate, framing, cable grade or loss budget has been set or checked at that rate.
findings.where: Frontend U1 (XC7A35T-2CSG325I) GTP TX0 balls H2 (P) / H1 (N); TX1-TX3 unconnected, RX balls on GND. J3 pin 5 = GTP_TX0_P, pin 3 = GTP_TX0_N (swap intended, TXPOLARITY=1). Micro-HDMI cable, about 1.8 m. HDMI Extension Board J610-J617 pins 3/5 -> ESD U801-U808 -> AC capacitors C745-C760 -> MC3 GTY RX quads 224/226 (rec_rx[0..7]).
findings.evidence: inputs/hdmi/design_inputs/START_HERE.md line 17: 256 Mbit/s per port, about 1.25 Gb/s (assumed), 800 ps; line 34: skew and spacing items to be reopened if the rates are higher; line 36: cable about 1.8 m. inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md line 31: one GTP TX lane at about 1.25 Gb/s (its line 28 lists 64 DATA lines). inputs/frontend/V2_review_fixes/Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc and exports/frontend/nets.csv: 64 nets ASIC1-8_DATA1-8, J1/J2 to U1. ASIC_REFERENCE.md section 3, line 51: 256 Mbit/s raw, 192 Mbit/s payload per ASIC; x 8 = 2.048 Gb/s raw, 1.536 Gb/s payload. Reference clocks are 125 MHz on both ends (Frontend Y1 AX3DAF1-125.0000T3; the XEM's on-module oscillator for rec_refclk). With UG482 dividers the reachable lane rates are 1.875, 2.0, 2.5, 3.125 and 3.75 Gb/s. 8b/10b payload: 1.25 -> 1.0 Gb/s (too low); 2.0 -> 1.6 Gb/s (96 % load with packed data, too tight); 2.5 -> 2.0 Gb/s (77 % packed); 3.125 -> 2.5 Gb/s (82 % raw). Nyquist frequency rises from 0.625 GHz to 1.25-1.56 GHz. The Frontend schematic note lists 'GT link rate/protocol, cable SI' as unverified; no later lane-rate decision was found in inputs/ or the 3-11 Nov dated folders.
findings.source: ASIC reference V1 (inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md) section 3, line 51; AMD DS181 v1.27.1 Table 52 (GTP maximum 6.25 Gb/s for -2 in CS/CP packages; PLL range 1.6-3.3 GHz; line rate 3.2-6.6 Gb/s at output divider 1), https://www.amd.com/content/dam/xilinx/support/documents/data_sheets/ds181_Artix_7_Data_Sheet.pdf; AMD UG482 7 Series GTP Transceivers, PLL dividers; engineering judgement. The HDMI cable-category limit was quoted from memory and not re-read.
findings.consequence: If cables or firmware are planned around 1.25 Gb/s, the link cannot carry eight ASICs. At 2.5-3.125 Gb/s a thin 1.8 m Micro-HDMI cable with its ESD parts and connectors may not give an open eye, which shows up as bit errors and lost recording frames on some ports.
findings.suggested_action: Record the lane rate and framing (2.5 Gb/s with packed 12-bit data, or 3.125 Gb/s with raw frames) and reopen the HDMI-board items tied to the rate. Run an IBERT eye and loss check over one real cable at 1.25-1.56 GHz Nyquist before buying eight sets.

findings.title: No record estimates or limits head-stack heat; about 1.45 W per stack gives a 19-34 K still-air surface rise.
findings.what: Nearly all power that enters a stack becomes heat in it: the FPGA, the 5 V-to-3.3 V buck and the other bucks, the linear regulators and the ASIC boost converter. The Option A stack is small (24.12 x 47.05 x 13.82 mm), so in still air its average surface rises about 19-34 K at the expected 1.45 W, with hot spots over U1 and the bucks running higher. Eight stacks stand side by side on the animal's skull with probe shanks in the brain, so they heat each other and the head, about 11.6 W in total at the expected load. No record sets a temperature limit, and only a measurement of one powered stack running the real bitstream will give the real rise.
findings.where: Frontend U1 (XC7A35T), U16 and U2/U3/U4/U13 (MPM3833C), U5/U6 (TPS74801), U10 (MP5077); FPGA-LDO A U1 (LT3582-12), U2/U6/U8/U9 (LT3042), U10 (LT3094), U3/U4/U5/U7 (TPS7A2015); four ASIC boards per stack; whole Option A stack (Option B is larger and similar).
findings.evidence: a review working file (not published) 1.45 W expected, 2.79 W high at VIN_5V; rail currents match inputs/hdmi/power_estimate/START_HERE.md section 1 and inputs/asic/J3_pinout__Power_Budget.csv. A low case of about 1.1 W follows from the record's low column plus the boost. Envelope 24.12 x 47.05 x 13.82 mm (inputs/system/README_2026-11-11.md; matches Option_A_Head_Stack_V12.stl without the plug) -> 4,237 mm2. h = 10-15 W/m2K -> 15.7-23.6 K/W -> 23-34 K at 1.45 W, 17-26 K at 1.1 W, 44-66 K at 2.8 W. A convection plus radiation estimate gives h about 13-16 W/m2K, so about 19-23 K expected. The 2.8 W case assumes all 1,024 stimulators at 22.5 uA on both rails continuously and VCCINT 0.4 A; with 1 ms pulses under 200 Hz and one rail per phase it falls to about 2.1 W (about 33 K). Option B (27.90 x 52.88 x 13.77 mm, 5,175 mm2) rises about 20 % less. Eight stacks: 9-22 W, 11.6 W expected. inputs/system/weekly_deck/START_HERE.md (11 Nov 08:24 entry): eight stacks on a sheep skull, shanks in the brain. A search of inputs/ found no head-stack thermal estimate or limit.
findings.source: Engineering judgement (lumped surface model). The IEC 60601-1 applied-part surface limit of about 43 C for long contact is from secondary sources and was not read; tissue-heating limits (usually about 1-2 K brain temperature rise) are stricter. Efficiency curves of the LT3582-12, MPM3833C and TPS74801 were not checked against the datasheets.
findings.consequence: Stack surfaces above body-contact limits, heat conducted down the shanks into the brain, and hot FPGA and ASIC junctions; the planned commercial-grade U1 (XC7A35T-2CSG325C, 0-85 C) leaves less junction margin. This may force a heat sink, duty cycling or a head-mount change after eight stacks are built.
findings.suggested_action: Set a head-surface and tissue-heating limit, then measure one powered stack (thermocouple or IR) in still air with the real bitstream before ordering eight.

findings.title: Frontend JTAG uses HDMI pin 2 for TMS, a wire that cables without Ethernet may leave out.
findings.what: The Frontend's JTAG runs as single wires in the roughly 1.8 m HDMI cable: TMS on pin 2 (Utility/HEAC+), TDI on 15 (CEC), TCK on 17 (SCL) and TDO on 18 (SDA). findings.title: The FPGA cannot switch or monitor the ASIC rails or +/-12 V converter; they are on whenever the cable is live.
findings.what: On the FPGA-LDO boards the shared enable for all nine ASIC regulators and the LT3582 +/-12 V converter is only a resistor and capacitor from VIN_3V3, and VIN_3V3 itself is always on once the cable is powered. No enable signal comes from the FPGA and no power-good (a regulator's 'output is in range' signal) goes back, so the FPGA cannot hold off, sequence, watch or shut down the ASIC supplies, and swapping an ASIC board means pulling the cable or hot-plugging. The back-powering at start-up claimed in the original does not happen: the ASIC rails rise about 15-22 ms after VIN_3V3, well after the FPGA's 1.5 V I/O bank (about 3 ms), while the FPGA pins are still undriven. Power-down order is not settled by the files and needs a scope capture; the open point is whether the ASIC designer's still-unknown sequencing and pin limits require FPGA control, which is cheap to add only before ordering.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO A and Option B LDO board: R1 (10k to /VIN_3V3), C3 (4.7 uF), /EN_ASIC_RAILS to U1 (LT3582-12) pin 8 SHDN and U2-U10 EN; R19 (10k, /CHIP_RESET_SHARED J2.58 to /ASIC_DVDD); PG pins of U2, U6, U8, U9, U10 unconnected. Frontend: U16 (VIN_3V3, EN on VIN_5V), U2 PG_CORE_1V0 to U4 EN (VCCO_1V5), U1 ball C9. Spare joint pins J1.29-33, 35-37, 39, 43, 45, 47, 49 and J2.40/42 on Frontend and LDO boards. 'EN_ASIC_RAILS' appears 0 times in every connectors.csv. exports/frontend/netlist.xml: U16 EN = VIN_5V; U2 EN = VIN_3V3; U2 PG = PG_CORE_1V0 to U4 EN; FPGA_PUDC_B tied to VCCO_1V5 through R25 470R, so FPGA I/O stay 3-stated with pull-ups off until configuration. VCCO_1V5 is up about 2.7 ms after VIN_3V3 (MPM3833C 1.3 ms soft-start, 100 us PG delay). R19 can inject at most 1.5 V / 10k = 0.15 mA, against the DS181 10 mA clamp-current limit. STIM_EN_SHARED (Frontend U1.J6, J2.63) has R2 10k to GND on the LDO board, so stimulation enable defaults low. exports/hdmi/netlist.xml: PORT_ENABLE = U700.13 PG and U701-U708 pin 3.

findings.consequence: The FPGA cannot sequence the ASICs, keep them off during FPGA bring-up, shut down the +/-12 V converter or react to a failed rail. If the ASIC turns out to need a set power order, adding control after ordering changes the J1/J2 contract on both the Frontend and the LDO board; meanwhile ASIC boards can only be changed with the cable unplugged or by hot-plugging onto live rails.
findings.suggested_action: Get the ASIC power-up and power-down order and powered-off pin limits from the ASIC designer, and decide before ordering whether the FPGA gates the rails; if so, route a Frontend-driven enable on a spare pin (for example J1.29) to EN_ASIC_RAILS with R1 as a pull-down and return a wired-OR power-good. If not, write 'cable unplugged before any DF40 is mated or unmated' into the bring-up procedure and capture the power-down order on a scope.
findings.v2note: SYS-10's 2-contact enable/power-good fix has to be reserved during the pin map V6 allocation. V6 as traced takes 12 of the 15 spare Frontend-to-FPGA-LDO contacts (J1.29-33, 35-37, 39, 43, 45, 47, 49, J2.40, J2.42) and leaves 3: enough for enable and power-good, but not for the near chips' 4 DISC_OUT lines, which fit only if the FPGA-LDO board joins the top chips' SPI_CLK/SPI_LATCH (pins 72/70) to the near board's shared ones (63/61); V6 would then need 8 contacts instead of 12. The power-good half also needs regulator changes: PGFB is tied to IN on all five LT3042/LT3094 (U2, U6, U8, U9, U10), which the data sheets say disables power good, and the four TPS7A2015 rails (VDD_ADC, VDD_DRIVER, DVDD, VDD_CGEN) and the LT3582-12 have no PG pin, so a wired PG line reports no rail as built and at most 5 of the 9 rails even after PGFB dividers are added.
findings.upd_note: The ASIC designer said on 12 Nov 2026 that the power-up and power-down order does not matter and that signals on an unpowered chip do not matter, so the FPGA does not have to switch the rails. Pin map V6 carries no enable or power-good line, and on FPGA-LDO A layout V14 all rails still turn on from the 3.3 V input alone. What remains: the FPGA cannot switch off or see a failed rail, only one spare contact is left for a later change, and the rule to unplug the cable before an ASIC board is fitted or removed is not yet written down.

findings.title: An open or wrong SET resistor drives an ASIC rail to about 3.2 V or +/-11.7 V, and nothing clamps it.
findings.what: The LT3042 and LT3094 regulators set their output as 100 uA times one SET resistor to AGND. If that 0402 resistor is open or the wrong value, the output ramps toward the input minus dropout, and every rail goes to all eight ASICs on a head with no clamp. The unused power-good (PG) pins are left the way the data sheet allows, and PG only flags a low output, so wiring it would not catch this fault; the inherited LDO Board A had the same exposure on nine rails. The ASIC's absolute voltage limits are not known, so the files cannot say whether this damages the ASICs; only limits from the ASIC designer would settle it.
findings.where: LDO A and LDO B LDO board: U2/R201 (ASIC_VDD_FE), U6/R601 (ASIC_REF_VDD), U8/R801 (ASIC_REF_VCM), U9/R901 (ASIC_VDD10), U10/R1001 (ASIC_VSS10); rails reach J3/J4 pins 50, 52, 40, 36, 54 directly.

Inputs: U2, U6, U8 on VIN_3V3 (3.32 V from Frontend U16, R59 200k / R60 44.2k, 0.6 V feedback from memory); U9, U10 on STIM_PRE_POS/NEG from LT3582-12 +/-12 V through bridged JP1/JP2. findings.source: ADI LT3042 data sheet (copy footer 3042fa), p.12 Pin Functions (SET, PG, PGFB), p.14 Output Voltage (0 V to VIN minus dropout), p.18 Programmable Power Good, https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/lt3042.pdf (direct download timed out; text from the copy in the review scratch folder); LT3094 data sheet, same PG/PGFB guidance; inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md items U02/U03.

findings.suggested_action: Make it a bring-up rule to measure every rail at J3/J4 with no ASIC board mated, after assembly and after any rework. An overvoltage supervisor or clamp is optional and needs the ASIC limits first.

findings.title: A port in current limit leaves the Frontend browned out, not shut down, and the XEM cannot see the fault.
findings.what: Frontend buck module U16 (MPM3833C) has its enable pin tied straight to VIN_5V, so it keeps running down to its own input lockout of 2.3-2.75 V. If a port's TPS2553 switch limits current, VIN_5V sags and U16 can sit in dropout (input too low to regulate) with VIN_3V3 partly up, while the TPS2553 stays in current limit and cycles on its 135 C thermal shutdown. Each FAULT output drives only an LED, so the XEM8310 cannot see or clear a port fault. findings.title: ASIC rail regulators have no set current limit, so a fault shared by eight ASICs can draw 160-730 mA.
findings.what: All five LT3042/LT3094 regulators have their current-limit pin (ILIM) tied to ground, so only their internal limit applies (about 220-320 mA at low input voltage). The four TPS7A2015 regulators have no limit pin; their internal limit is 360-730 mA, folding back to about 160 mA into a hard short. Each regulator feeds all eight ASICs, which normally draw only 1.4-18 mA per rail in total. One resistor on ILIM would cap an LT3042 rail at about 50 mA, but that limit would still be shared by eight ASICs, and no file or datasheet shows that the present limits would fuse bond wires.

findings.title: One open feedback resistor (R700) lets the HDMI board's shared 5 V rail run up to about 12 V, with no overvoltage stop or clamp.
findings.what: R700 is the 40.2 kOhm resistor from the 5 V output to the U700 module's feedback pin. If it is missing, tombstoned or cracked, or if R701 is shorted, the feedback pin sees 0 V and the module drives its output to just below its 12 V input. The module has no overvoltage stop of its own, its power-good output reads the same feedback pin, and nothing clamps FE_5V. Power-good does keep the eight port switches off, but each switch then holds about 12 V on its input against a 7 V absolute maximum, with no stated behaviour. This settles the 'TPS2553 with about 12 V if R700 opens' item in the system not-checked list.
findings.where: HDMI Extension Board V37: U700 TPSM63606 pin 10 (FB). R700 40.2k 0603 at (129.4, 60.9), about 3 mm from the module, from FE_5V to FB. R701 10k from FB to DGND; C708 22 pF across R700. FE_5V feeds U701-U708 (TPS2553) IN; PORT_ENABLE = U700.13 PG; TP700 (FE_5V) at (134.25, 65.5). Downstream: Frontend U16 MPM3833C on VIN_5V.

No diode, TVS or clamp on FE_5V; the only diodes on the board are D500 (USBLC6-2SC6) and the LEDs D701-D708. Setpoint 1 V x (1 + 40.2k/10k) = 5.02 V. With R700 open, FB sits at 0 V and the output rises toward the input; estimated 11.5-11.9 V at 12 V in. PG is derived from FB (94-107 % window, 120 us filter), so PG stays low and holds PORT_ENABLE low. findings.title: On the ASIC board the clock and strobe lanes switch between the AGND and DGND planes with no tie between them.
findings.what: A fast signal's return current flows in the ground plane right under its trace. On the ASIC board the top-layer clock lanes run over the AGND (analog ground) plane and the bottom-layer lanes over the DGND (digital ground) plane, so at each through via the return current must jump between the two grounds. No capacitor or tie joins AGND and DGND on the board, so the return goes either through the rail decoupling capacitors and the capacitance between the stacked rail planes, or out through the J3/J4 ground contacts to the net tie NT1 on the LDO board. Either way, clock-edge current passes through the analog rails and AGND of a recording chip. How much noise this causes can only be judged by measurement.

findings.title: Eight stacks need PCIe Gen3 x4 to the host, but no record states Gen3 or packed samples as a requirement.
findings.what: Eight stacks of eight ASICs produce 12.3 Gb/s (1.54 GB/s) of packed 12-bit samples, or 16.4 Gb/s (2.05 GB/s) if each sample is sent as a 16-bit word, before framing. The only host path that can carry this is the HDMI Extension Board's PCIe x4 link; at Gen2 it cannot carry 16-bit words and has almost no margin for packed data, while Gen3 carries either, and the XEM8310 USB 3 interface is several times too slow. Every part of the chain already supports Gen3 x4 (the FPGA's PCIe block, the Thunderbolt adapter and the board layout), so the open generation is a firmware IP setting plus a bring-up test, not a copper change. The project record states the system rate (about 2 GB/s) but does not tie it to the host-link generation or record a fallback.

findings.title: The ASICs are powered about 7 s before the Frontend is configured, with their clock and SPI inputs floating.
findings.what: On both FPGA-LDO A and the Option B LDO board, one RC (R1/C3) enables every ASIC regulator 15-22 ms after VIN_3V3 rises, whatever the FPGA is doing. The Frontend has PUDC_B strapped high, which turns off the FPGA's internal pull-ups during configuration, so the FPGA-driven ASIC clock (CLKH), SPI clock and SPI data lines float at the powered ASICs until configuration ends about 7 s later. Floating CMOS inputs can draw extra current and toggle at random. The files cannot settle whether this is safe, because the ASIC reset polarity and safe input states are unknown; an answer from the ASIC designer would settle it.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO A and Option B LDO board: R1 10k / C3 4.7 uF on /EN_ASIC_RAILS (U1 LT3582 SHDN, U2/U6/U8 LT3042, U9/U10 LT3094, U3/U4/U5/U7 TPS7A2015 EN); R2-R5, R16, R17, R18 10k pull-downs; R19 10k CHIP_RESET_SHARED pull-up to ASIC_DVDD. No pull on any board: BOARD1_CLK, BOARD3_CLK, BOARD1_SPI_CLK, BOARD3_SPI_CLK, STIM_CHIP1..4_SPI_DL/DR (Frontend U1 balls G16, V17, D10, V8, C11, G14, C14, C16, V7, V6, N17, N18; ASIC board CLKH, SPI_CLK, SPI_DINL/DINR). Frontend R25 470R PUDC_B to VCCO_1V5.
findings.evidence: exports/ldo_a/netlist.xml and exports/ldo_b_ldo/netlist.xml: /EN_ASIC_RAILS has 13 nodes (R1, C3, TP4, U1.8, U2-U10). The clock and SPI nets are 2-node nets on every LDO and router board, go straight to U1 balls on the Frontend and reach the ASIC pins with no resistor (exports/asic/netlist.xml). Enable delay t = 47 ms x ln(3.3/(3.3-V)): 15 ms at 0.9 V (TPS7A20 VEN(HI) max) and 22 ms at 1.24 V (LT3042 EN/UV rising, 1.18/1.24/1.32 V). Configuration: U12 hold 1.07 s (TPS3890 1.07 s per uF, C84 1 uF) plus 17,536,096 bits / 3 MHz = 5.85 s, about 7 s in total. inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md rows U03/U05 and line 76: reset polarity and pad limits unknown.
findings.source: AMD UG470, 7 Series FPGAs Configuration User Guide: PUDC_B high disables I/O pull-ups during configuration (not opened, docs.amd.com returned 404; from memory). ASIC reference V1, rows U03/U05. Analog Devices LT3042 datasheet, EN/UV threshold row; TI TPS7A20 datasheet, VEN(HI) row; TI TPS3890 datasheet SLVSD65A, p.3.
findings.consequence: Powered ASICs with floating inputs may draw extra current and may clock random data into the configuration shift register, and whether CHIP_RESET held high and FE_RESET held low is a safe state is unknown. Boot also takes about 7 s unless the bitstream raises the configuration clock.
findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer for the reset polarity and the safe idle state of CLKH and SPI, then add pull-downs on the LDO board for the floating lines rather than setting PUDC_B low, whose weak pull-ups would fight the 10k pull-downs on STIM_EN, STIM_START and FE_RESET. Set BITSTREAM.CONFIG.CONFIGRATE as high as the U8 translator timing allows.
findings.v2note: With the ASIC boards V4, SYS-28 is broader. The far (top) chips have their own SPI clock (pin 72), latch (pin 70) and two data lines per chip (66/68 and 16/18), so pin map V6 adds 6 FPGA-driven lines per port. That is 12 per head stack, or 24 unpulled FPGA-to-ASIC lines with the existing 12, and all of them float for about 7 s while PUDC_B is high. The two new latch lines (T_SPI_LATCH) also lack the 10k pull-down that R18 gives SPI_LATCH_SHARED on FPGA-LDO A and the Option B LDO board. During the V6 re-route, add a pull-down on each far latch (or tie it to SPI_LATCH_SHARED if the ASIC designer confirms the latch may be shared), and decide whether the far SPI clock and data lines need pulls. On today's V5-based files these far-chip inputs sit on FPGA input balls and float permanently, which is part of blocker A-P. See SYS-62.
findings.upd_note: On FPGA-LDO A layout V16 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 09:49 CST the 10k pull-downs stay on both CLKH lines, all four SPI clocks and all three SPI latches (R18, R20 to R27); the owner confirmed on 13 Nov 2026 that R20 to R23 are kept. So floating data can no longer be clocked or latched into the chips before the FPGA is configured. The ASIC designer said on 12 Nov 2026 that power-up order and unpowered inputs do not matter and that the pads have no internal pulls. Still open: the 16 SPI data inputs have no pull and float for about 7 s, the reset polarity was not answered, and the boot clock is still 3 MHz.

findings.title: Clock and strobe edges may overshoot the 1.5 V ASIC rail by up to 0.4 V, and the ASIC pad limits are unknown.
findings.what: The FPGA drives the shared clock and strobe lanes with no series resistor, and the ASIC dies at the far ends are light loads, so the edges ring above the 1.5 V rail and below ground. A simple lossless model (no clamp diodes) puts the peak up to about 0.4 V over the rail at a 1.0 ns edge; about 0.6 V is reached only with a pessimistic 5 nH connector loop. That much overshoot is ordinary for unterminated CMOS, and at 0.4 V or less a silicon clamp diode conducts only a little, so current through the input protection on every edge is not shown. The real gap is that the ASIC's input absolute-maximum and clamp limits are not published; only the ASIC designer can say whether the pads tolerate this.
findings.where: U01_BCD1/U01_BCD2 CLKH, SPI_CLK, FPGA_CLK (STIM_CLK), SPI_LATCH, RRST_DIGITAL/RST_DRIVER pads on all four ASIC boards; nets BOARD1/3_CLK, BOARD1/3_SPI_CLK, STIM_CLK_SHARED, SPI_LATCH_SHARED, CHIP_RESET_SHARED.
findings.evidence: a review working file (not published) at 1.0 ns rise, 20-30 ohm source and 0.8 nH contacts, peaks across all seven nets are 1.51 V (SPI_LATCH/STIM_CLK, eight dies, 30 ohm) to 1.93 V (B_BOARD1_CLK, 20 ohm, 2 pF). Re-run (a review working file (not published)): BOARD1_CLK at 1.0 ns/20 ohm gives 1.88 V at 0.8 nH, 2.13 V at 5 nH, 2.20 V at 8 nH; 1.62 V at 30 ohm/0.8 nH; 1.51-1.56 V at 1.5 ns/45 ohm. Undershoot below 0 V is the same size only in this linear model. exports/frontend/nets.csv and exports/ldo_a/nets.csv: no series resistors; LDO A has only 10k resistors to a rail or GND (R5/R18/R19). exports/asic/nets.csv: nets touch only J3/J4/U01_BCD1/U01_BCD2. ASIC_REFERENCE.md line 130: DVDD 1.5 V; line 175 (U03): VIH/VIL, absolute-maximum and clamp limits absent. The 45 ohm for DRIVE 8 is the DS181 worst-case bound (VOL 25 % of VCCO at 8 mA), not a typical value; the SLOW-slew edge rate is not verified (no IBIS model).
findings.source: inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md item U03; AMD DS181 Artix-7 Data Sheet v1.27.1, Table 4 (HR I/O overshoot VCCO + 0.55 V and undershoot -0.40 V for 100 % of the unit interval) and Table 8 (LVCMOS15 VOL), engineering judgement.
findings.consequence: If the ASIC pads tolerate only about 0.3 V outside their rail, the upper end of this overshoot could stress the input protection of dies that cannot be replaced, and the damage would be hard to trace.
findings.suggested_action: Ask the ASIC designer for the pad absolute-maximum and clamp ratings. Meanwhile use DRIVE 8 SLEW SLOW and probe CLKH at the far die's bond finger at first power-up with a probe of 1 GHz or more.
findings.upd_note: Pin file V3 now sets DRIVE 8 and SLEW SLOW on all 32 FPGA-to-ASIC outputs, the interim step this finding asked for; in the review's simple model that keeps the peak at about 1.5 to 1.6 V. The question was put to the ASIC designer on 12 Nov 2026, but the answer on pad limits and static protection was unclear, so the pads are treated as unprotected. Still open: the pad limits in writing, no series resistor on any of these lines, and a probe check of CLKH at the far chip at first power-up.

findings.what: The solder paste openings in the stencil (the metal sheet that prints paste onto the pads) are the same size as the copper pads on every DF40 connector in the stack. Hirose recommends a 0.12 mm stencil with an 80 % opening on both the receptacle (DS) and header (DP) halves, and warns that excess solder and flux can wick into the contacts. No pad, footprint or board paste margin or ratio is set anywhere, and the order notes give no stencil instruction.

findings.title: Neither the Frontend nor the FPGA-LDO A order asks for the 0.02 mm board flatness Hirose requires under each DF40, although both boards carry unbalanced copper.
findings.what: Hirose allows at most 0.02 mm of board warpage at the centre of each DF40, measured against the connector's ends. Over these 16.6-18.6 mm connectors that is about four to six times tighter than a common 0.75 % bow allowance. Every head joint has only 0.45 mm of effective engagement, and the Frontend-to-LDO joint uses two parallel 70-pin pairs. The Frontend has more plane copper above its centre core than below it, FPGA-LDO A pairs a 71 % plane with a 13 % signal layer, and the ASIC boards carry 63 % top against about 20 % bottom outer copper. No order note states a flatness or bow/twist limit, and JLC publishes none.
findings.where: Frontend J1/J2 (DF40C-70DS, bottom; 16.6 mm bodies, 17.5 mm apart). FPGA-LDO A J1/J2 (70DP, top), J3 (80DP, top) and J4 (80DS, bottom). ASIC V4 J3/J4 (18.6 mm). Order notes: inputs/frontend/V3_order/JLC_ORDER_NOTES.txt and inputs/ldo_a/V12_order/JLC_Remarks_paste.txt.
findings.evidence: Per-layer copper = pours (exports/<board>/zones.csv) plus track area (board.json), outer pads excluded. Frontend L1-L14: 8, 81, 78, 71, 3, 2, 78, 3, 78, 5, 78, 5, 81, 4 %. Mirror pairs are unbalanced at L3/L12 (78/5), L6/L9 (2/78) and L7/L8 (78/3, across the centre core); planes sit on L2/L3/L4/L7 above the core against L9/L11/L13 below; the dielectric stack is symmetric (exports/frontend/stackup.txt). LDO A L1-L6: 39, 71, 89, 89, 13, 51 %. ASIC V4: L2-L9 75-85 %; F.Cu 237 mm2 (63 %) against B.Cu 67 / 79 mm2 (18 / 21 %) (board_stats.txt). Bow arithmetic (a review working file (not published)): a 0.75 % bow sags 0.081 mm over a 16.6 mm DF40 on the 25.42 mm Frontend and 0.118 mm over 18.6 mm on the 22 mm ASIC board; Hirose's 0.02 mm equals about a 0.13-0.27 % bow. The order notes only ask that via-in-pad pads be 'flat and solderable'. The JLC capabilities page gives thickness ±10 % and outline ±0.1 / 0.2 mm, but no warpage figure.
findings.source: Hirose DF40 Series catalog, Jun 1 2024: p21 (board warpage 0.02 mm max at the centre relative to both connector ends; 2 reflows max) and p8 (A = 16.6 mm for 70 positions, 18.6 mm for 80), LCSC copy https://datasheet.lcsc.com/datasheet/pdf/145ab5d527b34eafa7a47375cb561c6a.pdf?productCode=C3640153. JLCPCB PCB capabilities, https://jlcpcb.com/capabilities/pcb-capabilities. The 0.75 % IPC-6012 SMT bow/twist figure is from memory, not re-read (paid standard).
findings.consequence: A board bowed beyond 0.02 mm across a DF40 can leave centre joints open after reflow. Two bowed boards also mate J1 and J2 unevenly inside the 0.45 mm engagement. Either fault would show only at bring-up as intermittent lines.
findings.suggested_action: Add to both order notes: 'flatness 0.02 mm max across each DF40 footprint (Hirose DF40 p21); please state your bow/twist limit'. Ask JLC whether it will add balancing copper on Frontend L8/L12 and LDO A L5, kept away from controlled lanes. Check the first bare boards on a surface plate before assembly.
findings.corrected: Neither the Frontend nor the FPGA-LDO A order note states a flatness requirement, although Hirose allows only 0.02 mm warpage at each DF40's centre and both boards have unbalanced copper (Frontend L3/L12 78/5 %, L6/L9 2/78 %, L7/L8 78/3 %; LDO A L2/L5 71/13 %). JLC's published limits (0.75 % for SMT boards, down to 0.5 % on special request) still allow roughly 0.05-0.08 mm of sag across a 16.6-18.6 mm DF40. The orders should ask for the tightest tolerance and name the 0.02 mm connector requirement, and the first bare boards should be checked flat.
findings.upd_note: The Frontend order remark (now for its panel, built on Frontend 14 layers V7 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 11:15 CST) still asks for 0.02 mm flatness along J1 and J2, bow and twist of 0.5 % or better, a report of the measured bow, and no balancing copper inside the outline. The FPGA-LDO A panel remark (for FPGA-LDO A layout V16 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 09:49 CST) still has no flatness line, and the ASIC boards V7, ten layers in 0.8 mm, have no order files yet. Each board now sits alone in a mostly bare 70 x 70 mm frame, whose effect on bow was not assessed. What remains: add the flatness request to the FPGA-LDO A and ASIC board orders and get the fabricators' bow and twist limits.

findings.title: DF40 joints are rated for 30 mating cycles, and no record says how often each stack will be unplugged.
findings.what: Hirose rates every DF40 for 30 mate/unmate cycles, with contact resistance at most 90 mOhm after them; nothing is specified beyond 30. The removable joints are the Frontend on the LDO A in Option A and the plug-in LDO board on the router in Option B, and the half that stays on the head wears with every swap. Several records state the 30-cycle rating, but none says how many unplugs are expected or keeps a mate count. This is a usage decision, not a board defect.
findings.where: Option A: Frontend J1/J2 mated to LDO A J1/J2 (70 positions). Option B: LDO board J5 mated to router J5 (120 positions).
findings.evidence: Hirose DF40 catalog, 2014 copy, p2: rated current 0.3 A; item 7 Durability, 90 mOhm max, 30 mating cycles. Hirose DF40 catalog, Jun. 1, 2024 copy, p5: mating durability 90 mOhm max, 30 times; rated current 0.3 A, 0.25 A for 120 positions. The 30-cycle rating is recorded in inputs/asic/sandwich_hub_options/START_HERE.md line 16, inputs/ldo_b/history/17_FPGA_LDO_B_Floorplan_V1_and_J5_Pin_Map_V2/START_HERE.md line 44, inputs/ldo_a/parts_review_V21/index.html (J5 row) and inputs/notes/fpga-ldo-v14.md line 52. inputs/system/weekly_deck/START_HERE.md assumes the Option A split (Frontend unplugs). No record gives an expected unplug count.
findings.source: Hirose DF40 Series catalog, 2014 copy, p2 item 7; Hirose DF40 Series catalog, Jun. 1, 2024, p5, https://www.hirose.com/en/product/series/DF40 (read from an LCSC-hosted copy).
findings.consequence: Past 30 cycles the contact resistance is no longer guaranteed, so the head-permanent board may need replacing after repeated swaps.
findings.suggested_action: Decide the expected number of unplugs per stack and keep a mate count per board at bring-up; if it exceeds the budget, plan to disconnect at the HDMI cable instead.

findings.already_known: inputs/asic/sandwich_hub_options/START_HERE.md discusses keeping a small part on the head (the reason for Option B).
findings.title: ASIC boards cannot be unplugged as Hirose requires, and Option A traps the FPGA-LDO board between ASIC pairs.
findings.what: Each ASIC board's DF40 connector sits near one long edge, with about 11.8 mm of board, dies and probes beyond it across the connector's width. With other boards 1.5 mm above and below, and only about 2.5-2.9 mm of board past each end of the connector, lifting a board evenly needs a thin tool; lifting the far end rocks the connector across its width, which Hirose prohibits. In Option A, replacing the FPGA-LDO board means unplugging the Frontend and both ASIC pairs, though each pair can come off as a mated unit.
findings.where: ASIC board: Edge.Cuts y 67.44-84.47; J3/J4 body about y 69.3-72.7 (J3 pads x 127.74-143.34, J4 pads x 127.27-143.82). FPGA-LDO Option A: J3 (DF40C-80DP, top) and J4 (DF40C-80DS, bottom) at (99.783, 113.51); J1/J2 take the Frontend.
findings.evidence: boards/asic/PCB.kicad_pcb Edge.Cuts x 124.34-146.31, y 67.44-84.47; exports/asic/pads.csv J3 pads y 69.47-72.55; 84.47 - 72.7 = 11.8 mm beyond the connector. exports/ldo_a/parts.csv: J3 and J4 both at (99.783, 113.51). Hirose DF40 unmating precautions (a review working file (not published)): lift evenly with both sides parallel; one-side lifting only on a very rigid board; do not pull on one side or a corner or from the width direction; connector is not meant as the main support.
findings.source: Hirose DF40 Series catalog, Feb. 2024 (LCSC copy), pp. 21 and 23, unmating precautions; same content re-checked in a 2014 catalog text, pp. 17-18 of that copy; https://www.hirose.com/en/product/series/DF40.
findings.consequence: Prying from the probe end can crack the DF40 housing or lift pads and puts tools next to bond wires and probe shanks. Option A service means handling the Frontend and two mated ASIC pairs.
findings.suggested_action: Before stacking boards with ASICs, define a spreader tool that separates boards evenly along the connector's long side and a written mate/unmate order, and weigh this in the Option A/B choice.
findings.upd_note: Option A is the build to finish first (decision of 12 Nov 2026), so the trapped FPGA-LDO board applies to the first heads. ASIC boards V7 are 0.8 mm thick and bend more easily than the 1.6 mm boards this finding was written on; the connector positions are unchanged. No tool and no mate and unmate order are on record.

findings.title: Enclosure V3 sets the HDMI Extension Board's height twice, by base posts and by the adapter's PCIe slot.
findings.what: In enclosure V3 the board is clamped between nine base posts and lid pins, and its card edge is also seated in the DFR1169 adapter's x16 slot, which is screwed to the back wall. So two separate chains of printed-part and vendor-part tolerances both fix the board's height (it is over-constrained). In plane, the board is also located twice, by a pin in one mounting hole and by the slot. Each Micro-HDMI insertion can push up to 44.1 N in plane, a load the record has not checked; holes MH2/MH3 exist on V37 but are not used.
findings.where: Enclosure V3: nine base posts (board underside z 0) and lid pins; adapter slot centre plane z 0.8 mm on 6 mm pillars, slot mouth y 154.454, nominal seating 7.6 mm; card fingers x 109.68-160.98; locating pin in the 3.5 mm hole at (164.68, 100.05); HDMI Extension Board V37 MH2/MH3.

findings.title: In Option A the FPGA-LDO A connectors J1/J2 stay open on the animal's head whenever the Frontend is unplugged, with no cover and no cleaning method.
findings.area: Connector exposure on the head (Option A)
findings.what: The project assumes an Option A split in which the Frontend unplugs and FPGA-LDO A stays on the head with the four ASIC boards. Between sessions, LDO A's two 70-contact DF40 headers then face hair, bedding, blood and saline. Hirose protects the contacts only when mated, does not recommend cleaning, and lists no cover, and no cover has been chosen. LDOB-22 records the same problem for Option B's J5 only.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO A J1 and J2 (DF40C-70DP-0.4V(51), top) at (91.255, 127.0) and (108.755, 127.0). They carry 108 ASIC and control signals, 14 GND and VIN_3V3 (J2.68-70), which is live again as soon as the Frontend is re-mated.
findings.evidence: inputs/system/weekly_deck/START_HERE.md line 67: 'the Option A split (Frontend unplugs, FPGA-LDO stays) is assumed'. exports/ldo_a/parts.csv: J1/J2 on the top side. known/system.json checked_ok: the 140 J1/J2 pins are 108 signals, 14 GND, 3 VIN_3V3 and 15 spares. No cover or dummy-plug part appears in any parts.csv or record.

findings.already_known: J5 having only three returns is known (S7 in parts review V21 / notes fpga-ldo-v14); the +/-10 V adjacency is not recorded.
findings.title: The +10 V and -10 V connector pins sit 0.4 mm from 1.5 V rail pins, and on LDO B J5 beside an ASIC data line.
findings.what: On every 80-pin DF40 connector J3/J4, the +10 V pin (VDD10) and the -10 V pin (VSS10) each have a 1.5 V rail pin on both sides, 0.4 mm apart. A solder bridge between neighbours would put 8.5 V or 11.5 V on 1.5 V rails shared by all eight ASICs on a head and on regulator outputs rated far below that. This pin order comes from the ASIC designer's pin table and is fixed by the ASIC board; nothing fails as drawn, so it is a bring-up and assembly hazard. The not-yet-ordered LDO B J5 repeats the pattern and puts VSS10 next to ASIC1_DATA4, which runs straight to an FPGA pin.

findings.title: No board has a test pad on any of the nine ASIC rails, so rails must be probed on small capacitor pads.
findings.what: Each of the nine ASIC rails should be measured before the first ASIC board is plugged in, but no board has a test point on any of them. The rails can still be reached on bottom-side regulator output capacitor pads on LDO A and the LDO B LDO board, and these stay reachable with the full stack mated, because the ASIC boards cover only up to about y 118.8 and the nearest rail capacitor is at y 121.9. Probing 0402 pads, or the 0.4 mm pitch DF40 contacts where DVDD pin 34 sits next to VDD10 pin 36, is slow and a probe slip can short neighbours. This is a bring-up convenience item, not a likely failure.

findings.title: The Frontend cable connector has no ESD protection on the GT pair, JTAG pins, sense pin or 5 V input.
findings.what: The head end of the cable is the one plugged and unplugged most, so it is where a static discharge from the cable is most likely. On the Frontend only the clock, command and SYNC LVDS pairs pass through an ESD array (U17, U18 TPD4E02B04). The transceiver (GT) transmit pair, the four JTAG lines, the sense line and the 5 V input go to the FPGA or the power input with no protection part. The HDMI Extension Board's ESD parts protect only that board, and on it the JTAG and sense lines pass only through 100 ohm resistors and an analog switch.
findings.where: Frontend: J3.3/5 GTP_TX0_N/P to U1 H1/H2 (no ESD, no AC capacitor on this board); J3.2/15/17/18 FPGA_JTAG_TMS/TDI/TCK/TDO to U1 R8/T9/F8/T8 (bank 0); J3.1 CABLE_TARGET_SENSE to R27 only; J3.19 VIN_5V with no TVS; U18 IO3/IO4 spare, tied to GND. HDMI Extension Board: J61x.1/2/15/17/18 to R640-R671 (100R) and U611-U617 (TS3A27518E); GT and LVDS pairs there have U801-U816.

findings.source: TI TPD4E02B04 data sheet SLVSD85B (Rev. B, July 2016), p.1 features (+/-12 kV contact, +/-15 kV air, 0.25 pF typical / 0.33 pF max) and section 7.3.4, https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/tpd4e02b04.pdf; engineering judgement.
findings.consequence: A cable discharge while plugging at the head can damage the GT transmitter or the configuration bank of a 14-layer HDI BGA board that is hard to rework.
findings.suggested_action: Accept for the first build with ESD handling rules (touch the shell first, plug with power off) and record it; in the next Frontend revision, use U18's two spare channels for TCK and TMS or add one TPD4E02B04 on the JTAG lines.

findings.title: The XEM can drive LVDS pairs into an unpowered Frontend, back-feeding its 1.5 V bank through clamp diodes.
findings.what: The XEM drives the clock, command and SYNC pairs on every port whenever its bitstream runs, but it cannot tell whether a port's Frontend is powered. On a live plug, or when a port is in fault or current limit, the Frontend's VCCO_1V5 rail is at or near 0 V, so up to 4 LVDS legs (6 on ports 3-6) push current through the Artix-7 clamp diodes (protection diodes from each pin to its bank supply) and can partly lift the dead rail. This does not happen on a normal cold start, because the ports power up about 10 ms after 12 V, before the XEM is configured. The files cannot settle how much current flows; the LVDS driver current is expected to stay below the 10 mA clamp limit, and a measurement of VCCO_1V5 during a live plug would settle it.
findings.where: HDMI Extension Board MC1 bank 64 (B64_L6P/N clock, B64_L5P/N command/SYNC, plus SYNC on ports 3-6) to J610-J617 pins 6/8, 9/11, 12/14, with ESD U801/U809; Frontend J3 to U1 P14/R15 (CABLE_CLK), M14/N14 (CMDSYNC), B9/A9 (SYNC) on VCCO_1V5, each with a 100 ohm resistor R61/R62/R64; PORT_ENABLE from U700.13 (PG) to U701-U708 EN; FAULT outputs to D701-D708 only.

findings.already_known: FT232H EEPROM ships blank: V35 prefab review (reviewer agrees).
findings.title: The Frontend FPGA can be configured only through the HDMI cable from a working HDMI Extension Board.
findings.what: JTAG is the four-wire test and programming port of the FPGA. On the Frontend, each JTAG net has just two pads, the FPGA ball and a contact on the Micro-HDMI connector, and the SPI flash can only be written through the FPGA. A first Frontend therefore needs a working HDMI Extension Board (USB-JTAG chip, switches set correctly, cable voltage check met) and a good cable; if any of these fails there is no fallback. A blank FT232H EEPROM mainly affects whether AMD's Vivado recognises the cable; open tools may still drive it (judgement, not checked).
findings.where: Frontend: U1 TCK F8, TMS R8, TDI T9, TDO T8; nets FPGA_JTAG_TCK/TMS/TDI/TDO to J3 pins 17/2/15/18; flash U7 via U8; FPGA_PROGRAM_B (no test pad); INIT_B on TP11. HDMI Extension Board: U501, U602, U603 (TPS3700DDCR), U610-U618, SW600.
findings.evidence: exports/frontend/nets.csv: FPGA_JTAG_* pad_count 2 (J3 and U1); FPGA_PROGRAM_B 3 pads (R17, U1.P10, U11.6); flash nets only to U7, U8 and pull resistors. exports/frontend/pads.csv: no TP on any JTAG net; R27 from VCCAUX_1V8 to CABLE_TARGET_SENSE (J3.1). exports/hdmi: R605 301k/R606 100k give 0.4 V x 401/100 = 1.604 V; R607 402k/R608 100k give 0.4 V x 502/100 = 2.008 V on U603. The HDMI board has no standalone JTAG header (J4, J500, J900-J911, J920 carry no JTAG net).
findings.source: AMD UG470 (7 Series FPGAs Configuration User Guide), JTAG and master SPI configuration; TI TPS3700 data sheet SBVS187 (0.4 V threshold not re-read); Engineering judgement.
findings.consequence: Bring-up of the first Frontend stalls on any HDMI Extension Board or cable problem, with no independent way to tell which side is at fault.
findings.suggested_action: Add four small JTAG pads plus GND and VCCAUX_1V8 on a Frontend edge before ordering, or document a Micro-HDMI breakout to a standard AMD 2 mm JTAG header.

findings.title: Once the head is stacked, FPGA configuration and the power-good/reset chain cannot be seen or probed.
findings.what: No board in the head (Frontend, LDO A, Option B router and LDO board, ASIC board) has an LED. The Frontend's only DONE pad, TP12 (DONE is the FPGA pin that goes high when configuration has loaded), is on the bottom side between J1 and J2, under the board that mates there. The power-good and reset nets, and a few internal supply nets, have no test pad at all. Most output rails and INIT_B can be probed on top, so the real gaps are DONE and the power-good/reset chain.

findings.title: STIM_EN, STIM_START, STIM_CLK and STIM_CHB reach all eight ASICs of a stack and the ASIC configuration cannot be read back, so an ASIC not loaded with a safe table can stimulate whenever another ASIC does.
findings.area: Stimulation control and SPI configuration (stimulation safety)
findings.what: Each of the four stimulation control lines (STIM_EN, STIM_START, STIM_CLK, STIM_CHB) is one FPGA net shared by all eight ASICs on a Frontend: both FPGA-LDO ports and both boards of each stack. CHIP_RESET is shared the same way. The only per-chip control is the configuration shifted in over SPI, whose stimulus tables hold a per-stimulator ENABLED field; the ASIC has no SPI output pin, so firmware cannot read back what a chip holds, and no record says what the stimulation registers contain after power-up or after CHIP_RESET. On today's pin-map-V5 hardware (FPGA-LDO A V12, Option B router V2) the far board's SPI clock, latch and data pins (16, 18, 66, 68, 70, 72) are plain lanes to FPGA inputs, so the four far ASICs of each stack are powered and clocked but can never be configured, yet they receive every stimulation pulse with whatever table they powered up with or picked up from their floating SPI lines. Option B's J5 has no spare pin, so there this state would be permanent; pin map V6 makes every chip loadable, but safety then rests entirely on firmware loading a safe table into all eight chips every time.

findings.consequence: A chip that powers up with stimulators enabled, or whose SPI load is corrupted (for example by the latch glitch in SYS-51 or by the floating top-chip latch in the separate pull-down finding), drives current into tissue whenever stimulation starts for any chip in the stack, and nothing in the system can detect it. A head built from FPGA-LDO A V12 or Option B V2 with far boards fitted can deliver unintended stimulation from up to four unconfigured chips per stack whenever the near chips stimulate, whatever the firmware does.
findings.suggested_action: Record now that far boards are not fitted to pin-map-V5 hardware (FPGA-LDO A V12, Option B V2) with stimulation enabled, and carry this into the Option B decision, because there the far chips can never be configured. Ask the ASIC designer what the stimulation registers hold after power-up and after CHIP_RESET, and whether an all-zero L/R stream disables every stimulator; then make it a firmware rule to load an all-disabled table into all eight chips after every power-up and CHIP_RESET, before STIM_EN is raised. Before freezing V6, decide whether one of the last spare joint contacts should split STIM_EN per port.
findings.corrected: STIM_EN, STIM_START, STIM_CLK and STIM_CHB (and CHIP_RESET and FE_RESET) each reach all eight ASICs on a Frontend. The die has no SPI output, so a chip's stimulus table cannot be read back, and no record says what the table holds after power-up or CHIP_RESET (ASIC_REFERENCE U05). Per-chip stimulation safety therefore rests entirely on firmware loading a known all-disabled table into every chip after each power-up and each CHIP_RESET, before STIM_EN rises, and that needs the ASIC designer's answer on reset contents and disable codes. On the pin-map-V5 boards (FPGA-LDO A V12, and Option B V2 through J5), the far chips' six SPI lines per port are already plain copper to bidirectional LVCMOS15 FPGA balls, so those chips stay unloaded only until the pin file and firmware change (known A-P), not permanently and not "whatever the firmware does".
findings.upd_note: With pin map V6, frozen by the owner on 13 Nov 2026 at 08:36 CST and built into FPGA-LDO A layout V16 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 09:49 CST, Frontend 14 layers V7 · edited 13 Nov 2026, 11:15 CST and ASIC boards V7, each of the eight chips has its own two SPI data lines to its own FPGA pins, and the top chips have their own SPI clock and latch with pull-downs. So every chip can be loaded with a safe table on its own, and the case of top chips that can never be configured is gone for Option A. What remains: STIM_EN, STIM_START, STIM_CLK and STIM_CHB, and both resets, are still one line each for all eight chips, and the configuration cannot be read back. The ASIC designer did not say what the stimulation registers hold after power-up or which table switches every stimulator off.

findings.title: No bring-up or handling procedure exists, yet 21 open items, four of them major, rely on one as their only protection for the first build.
findings.what: Many open items were accepted for the first build on condition that a rule is followed. Examples: cable last on and first off; orientation and near/far check before mating; rails measured before the first ASIC board; ESD grounding; VIO1 set before any bitstream. Apart from four HDMI-board notes and the VIO1 step, no such procedure exists in the project records. The ASIC boards are now kept as received, and V4 adds neither key nor marking, so for SYS-09 and R2S-04 the procedure is the only defence. This review adds further first-power checks: see the findings on the shared STIM lines, the R700 feedback resistor, the J3 5 V pad beside TCK, the top-chip SPI latch and blank flash, and a bench supply on TP14.

findings.suggested_action: Before any board is powered, write a one-page bring-up and handling order. HDMI board alone: FE_5V at TP700, VIO1, EEPROM. Each Frontend alone on a checked port: rails, JTAG, flash. Frontend plus FPGA-LDO without ASIC boards: nine rails, pin-to-pin resistance. Bare ASIC boards: marking, orientation, rails at the fingers. Bonded boards last, cable last on, with ESD grounding. Link each step to the item it closes.
findings.corrected: No written bring-up or handling procedure exists for the Frontend, the FPGA-LDO boards or the ASIC boards. Yet about 20 open items, including the majors SYS-09, SYS-10, LDOB-04 and LDOB-08, name a handling rule or a first-power check as their fix or interim measure. As drawn, V4 has no board mark and no key, so until the open keying item is closed, only a written orientation and near/far check guards against SYS-09/R2S-04. findings.title: Rocking either V4 ASIC board on or off with the cable live leaves +10 V or -10 V and three 1.5 V rails connected after all four ground contacts have opened.
findings.area: Hot plug at the ASIC joints
findings.what: On the 80-pin J3/J4 the only grounds (AGND 42/44, DGND 46/48) sit mid-row, with four rails on each side and VDD_CGEN on pin 1. When a board is rocked off from either end, the grounds open while the rail group on the far side is still mated. From the pin-80 end those are DVDD, VDD10, VDD_DRIVER, REF_VCM and VDD_CGEN; from the pin-1 end, VDD_FE, REF_VDD, VSS10 and VDD_ADC. Every joint in the stack has this order, because each board passes pin n to pin n. Nothing on the head can switch the rails off first (SYS-10). This is the J3/J4 counterpart of LDOB-24 on J5.
findings.where: Both V4 boards J3/J4 (pin 1 at x 143.34, pin 80 at x 127.74), plus FPGA-LDO A J3/J4 and Option B router J3/J4, which use the same order. Rails: 1 VDD_CGEN, 34 DVDD, 36 VDD10, 38 VDD_DRIVER, 40 REF_VCM, 50 VDD_FE, 52 REF_VDD, 54 VSS10, 56 VDD_ADC.
findings.evidence:
W2/a review working file (not published) on exports/asic_bottom/pads.csv (asic_top gives the same result), output rocking_out.txt. Method as in LDOB-24: rigid tilt about a line 0.5 mm past the end row; a contact opens at 0.45 mm separation.
Pin-80 end lifted: the last ground opens at 0.85 mm. REF_VCM, VDD_DRIVER, VDD10 and DVDD stay mated to 0.89/0.94/0.99/1.05 mm, VDD_CGEN to the end, and 35 signal contacts are still mated.

findings.title: On the Frontend cable connector, the 5 V pad sits 0.15 mm from the FPGA's TCK pad, and neither JTAG line has a series resistor.
findings.what: The cable pin map carries 5 V on pin 19 and reuses the neighbouring HDMI pins 17 and 18 for the FPGA's JTAG clock (TCK) and data out (TDO). On the Frontend, pad 19 is 0.15 mm from pad 17 in the same row, and contact 19 sits next to contact 18 inside the connector. Both JTAG nets go straight to FPGA bank 0, which is powered from VCCAUX_1V8. A solder bridge or bent contact would therefore put the port's 5 V, with up to about 0.7 A behind it, onto an FPGA pin rated for 10 mA of clamp current. At the HDMI board end the same pins have 100 ohm resistors, so only the Frontend end is exposed.

findings.title: Driving Frontend pin M15 low to switch off the GT rails instead resets and reloads the FPGA, in a loop.
findings.what: FPGA pin M15 drives EN_GTPWR_1V5, which through U15 enables buck U13; U13's power-good (PG, a pin that goes low when a regulator is off or out of regulation) is the only enable of U5, the transceiver supply regulator. U5's PG is tied with U4's into BOOT_RAILS_PG_3V3, the manual-reset input of reset chip U12, which then pulls PROGRAM_B and INIT_B low through U11 and erases the FPGA's configuration. With the FPGA blank, M15 floats, R58 pulls the enable high, the rails return and the FPGA reloads, so any design that drives M15 low repeats this about every 7 s. The 'shutdown function' promised in the U15 field cannot be used.

findings.title: Returned CLK32MHz lines have no series resistor, so a strong ASIC driver could overshoot the FPGA input limit.
findings.what: Each ASIC drives its 32 MHz recording clock point-to-point to an FPGA clock pin with no series resistor, and the FPGA captures data on the falling edge. In a linear model of the far-chip (ASIC3) path the edge stays clean, but a strong, fast driver peaks near 2.5 V, about 1 V over the bank, beyond AMD's allowance, while a 30 ohm, 1 ns driver stays under about 1.7 V. The files cannot settle this because the ASIC output drive is unknown; a probe measurement at bring-up or the ASIC designer's driver data would.

Near chip: ASIC1 CLK32MHZ (J4.45), Option A J4.45 to J2.59, Frontend J2.59 to U1.R2. The same applies to ASIC2 and ASIC4-8.

findings.title: Under pin map V6 as traced, ASIC3 and ASIC7 each bring READ, DATA7 and DATA8 into a different FPGA bank from their returned clock, breaking the Frontend's one-bank-per-ASIC rule.
findings.area: Pin map V6 / FPGA banks and ASIC capture clocking
findings.what: The Frontend was laid out so each ASIC's returned clock sits on a clock-capable ball in the same bank as its other ten lines, so each chip can be captured on its own I/O clock buffer, which reaches only its own bank (BUFIO) or its own clock region (BUFR). In V6 the far chips' READ, DATA8 and DATA7 come in on J3/J4 pins 28/30/32, whose lanes end on Frontend J1, so even after the four clock swaps ASIC3's clock is on P4 (bank 34) while its T_READ, T_D<8> and T_D<7> arrive on F18, F17 and G17 (bank 15), and ASIC7's clock is on N3 (bank 34) while the same three lines arrive on M16, L14 and K15 (bank 14). Bank 34 has only K5 and K6 free, the nearest balls for the two new DATA6 lines, and restoring one bank per group would mean moving 6 outputs and 6 inputs across the BGA; ASIC8 and ASIC4 can stay whole in banks 14 and 15. Capture still works at 32 MHz on a global clock buffer with timing constraints, so this constrains the firmware and the V6 routing choice; it is not a failure.
findings.where: Frontend U1 banks 14, 15 and 34. ASIC7: READ/DATA8/DATA7 on M16, L14, K15 (bank 14); the rest on K3, N3, M5, P6, P5, R6, R1 and K5 (bank 34). ASIC3: READ/DATA8/DATA7 on F18, F17, G17 (bank 15); the rest on T2, P4, T3, N6, N2, M6, L5 and K6 (bank 34). Returned clocks after the swaps: P4 (IO_L12P_T1_MRCC_34) and N3 (IO_L11P_T1_SRCC_34). FPGA-LDO A: J4 pins 28/30/32 go to J1.48/46/44, and J3 pins 28/30/32 go to J1.21/23/25. Spare joint contacts J2.40/J2.42; free bank-34 balls K5/K6. The rule is stated in inputs/frontend/V2_review_fixes/Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc line 2 and in the schematic V46 J1/J2 note.

merged.title: ASIC3 and ASIC7 READ/DATA8/DATA7 cannot move into bank 34: its only free balls, K5 and K6, are already needed for the two new DATA6 lines.
merged.area: V6 pin map: returned-clock bank grouping
merged.what: In V6 the top chips' READ, DATA8 and DATA7 arrive on J1 and land in bank 14 (ASIC7) and bank 15 (ASIC3). Their returned 32 MHz clocks land in bank 34 (N3 and P4 after the Frontend swaps). Bank 34 already uses 48 of its 50 I/O. K5 and K6, the only free balls, take ASIC7_DATA6 and ASIC3_DATA6, so V6 fills bank 34 and leaves no ball for the six split lines. A clock buffer driven by the returned clock (BUFIO or BUFR, which serve one bank or region only) cannot reach those lines, because banks 14/15 and bank 34 sit in different I/O columns. The only repair on the Frontend alone is to swap each split input with one of the same chip's V6 outputs in bank 34. That means twelve lanes crossing the whole BGA, and it rarely worked cleanly in the test.
merged.where: Frontend U1. ASIC7: J1.21/J1.23/J1.25 -> M16/L14/K15 (bank 14), clock J2.36 -> N3. ASIC3: J1.48/J1.46/J1.44 -> F18/F17/G17 (bank 15), clock J2.25 -> P4. merged.consequence: The pin file assumes each chip's inputs are captured in the bank of its returned clock. Unless firmware uses a global clock, 3 of the 11 inputs on ASIC3 and on ASIC7 cannot be captured that way. One choice: capture ASIC3 and ASIC7 (all 11 inputs each) on a BUFG or MMCM clock from N3/P4 and close 32 MHz timing in Vivado; no copper change is needed. merged.corrected: In V6, ASIC7's and ASIC3's READ/DATA8/DATA7 land in banks 14 and 15, while their returned clocks (N3, P4) and other inputs sit in bank 34. Bank 34 is full once K5/K6 take the two new DATA6 lines, so these six inputs cannot be clocked by a BUFIO/BUFR from their own clock. No copper change is needed: a BUFG capture at 32 MHz has more than 10 ns of margin, and ASIC7 can also use a BUFH because bank 14 sits beside bank 34. Record the capture clock in the V6 pin file instead of the 12-lane Frontend crossing, which came out clean in only 1 of 8 trials.

findings.title: Three head boards carry DF40s on both faces, so one face's connectors use Hirose's full two-reflow limit.
findings.what: Hirose allows DF40 connectors at most two reflow cycles (passes through the soldering oven) and at most 0.02 mm of board warpage across a connector. FPGA-LDO A, the Option B router and the ASIC board have DF40s on both faces, so the first face's connectors see both assembly reflows and any further reflow or hot-air rework exceeds the rating. The Frontend and the Option B LDO board are also double-sided with DF40s on one face, so their DF40s also use both cycles unless their face is reflowed last.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO A J1/J2/J3 (top), J4 (bottom); Option B router J3 (top), J4/J5 (bottom); ASIC board J4 (top), J3 (bottom); Frontend J1/J2 (bottom, 59 top parts); Option B LDO board J1/J2/J5 (top, 63 bottom parts).

findings.title: The animal's reference electrode is tied to the host PC and 12 V adapter grounds, with no isolation and no leakage rule on record.
findings.what: The ASIC boards' J1 pin (AGND, the reference connection) joins GND at NT1 on the FPGA-LDO board. That ground runs through each HDMI cable shield to the HDMI Extension Board's DGND, which is also the ground of the USB-C/Thunderbolt link, the PCIe edge and the 12 V adapter. No board carries an isolator, so mains leakage from the host, the adapters or another instrument touching the animal can return through the animal's tissue and its reference electrode. Many research rigs accept this, while commercial systems sell isolation for subject safety; the project has no rule either way.
findings.where: ASIC V4 boards J1.1 (/AGND) at (144.875, 68.28); NT1 on FPGA-LDO A (100.58, 121.0) and on the Option B LDO board; Frontend J3 shell and GND pins; HDMI board J610-J617 shells to DGND, J500 (USB-C) A1/A12/B1/B12, J6 PCIe edge, J4.2.

findings.title: A bench supply hot-connected to the Frontend's TP14 can ring VIN_5V to 7.5-8 V, while cable hot-plug stays below about 5.6 V.
findings.what: FE-19 left the cable hot-plug overshoot to a measurement. A circuit model that includes the port switch shows the overshoot is small. The TPS2553 limits its current within about 2 us, long before the cable inductance and the Frontend's input capacitors can ring, and the cable resistance damps the rest. The real exposure is a stiff bench supply clipped onto TP14 while it is already on, because nothing then limits the current.

findings.title: With the V4 ASIC boards, firmware must still follow the chip numbering, the reversed DATA order and the shared CLKH and control lines, but SPI data is now one DL/DR pair per chip, the far boards have their own SPI clock, latch and returned clock (pins 72, 70, 62 and 12), and the XDC records none of this and has no clock constraints.
findings.what: Facts the FPGA design needs, read from the files. ASIC numbers: on the FPGA-LDO underside port (J4), ASIC1 = near board U01_BCD1, ASIC2 = near U01_BCD2, ASIC3 = far U01_BCD1, ASIC4 = far U01_BCD2; on the top-side port (J3), ASIC5/6 near and ASIC7/8 far, same order. Within every chip, DATAL<4..1> arrive as DATA1..4 and DATAR<4..1> as DATA5..8. Each chip's returned clock is on the P side of an SRCC/MRCC clock-capable pair in the same bank as its data: R2, D13, P4, E16, R3, R16, N3, P15 for ASIC1..8; ASIC1/3/5/7 in bank 34, ASIC2/4 in bank 15, ASIC6/8 in bank 14. SPI: stream STIM_CHIP1 loads ASIC1 and ASIC3, CHIP2 loads ASIC2 and ASIC4, CHIP3 loads ASIC5 and ASIC7, CHIP4 loads ASIC6 and ASIC8 (stream number and ASIC number differ for 3 and 4); BOARD1_SPI_CLK clocks ASIC1-4, BOARD3_SPI_CLK ASIC5-8, one SPI_LATCH for all eight. CLKH: BOARD1_CLK to ASIC1-4, BOARD3_CLK to ASIC5-8. STIM_EN, STIM_START, STIM_CLK, STIM_CHB (both CHBL and CHBR), CHIP_RESET (RRST_DIGITAL and RST_DRIVER), FE_RESET (RST_FEL and RST_FER) and IMP_TST go to all eight. No FPGA pin sees any DISC_OUT; AC_IN is only a 10k to AGND and TP7. The XDC has pin locations only: no create_clock or input-delay constraints for the eight returned clocks.
findings.where: inputs/frontend/V2_review_fixes/Frontend_V46_pins_V2.xdc; FPGA-LDO A / router J3/J4; V3 boards U01_BCD1/U01_BCD2.

findings.title: Each stack has a one-way transceiver lane and no reset line, so recovery needs firmware or a manual switch.
findings.what: Each cable carries one transceiver pair (a multi-gigabit serial lane), from the Frontend to the XEM only; the Frontend's receive pairs are grounded. The cable also carries JTAG (the programming and debug port) but no reset or PROGRAM line, and JTAG reaches one port at a time, chosen only by hand on rotary switch SW600. All eight port power switches also share one enable. A hung Frontend can therefore be recovered only by a command its firmware still decodes, by turning SW600 and sending a JTAG reprogram, or by a whole-system power cycle, and updating the flash on eight Frontends takes eight switch changes.
findings.where: Frontend U1 MGTPRX0-3 (E4/E3, A4/A3, C4/C3, G4/G3) on GND; Frontend J3 pins 3/5 GTP_TX0, 2/15/17/18 JTAG. HDMI Extension Board MC3 bank 224/226 TX pins unconnected, bank 224 RX0 to J610 pins 3/5 via C745; SW600 (SEL_0..SEL_8, pull-ups R620-R628) to U610-U618 pin 20; PORT_ENABLE = U700.13 to U701-U708 EN.

The receiver's lock time must come from the XEM8310's UltraScale+ data sheet (DS931); the DS181 Table 55 figure (2.3 x 10^6 UI, 0.92 ms at 2.5 Gb/s) is for the Artix-7 GTP and does not apply to the receiver.

findings.title: The relayed start-up order loads SPI before CLKH starts, but the only recorded working firmware ran CLKH continuously and clocked its SPI engine from the returned clock, which exists only while CLKH runs.
findings.area: ASIC start-up order and SPI clock source
findings.what: The relayed designer answer is: send SPI, reset the digital and analog sections, then start the recording clock. The original slides say the FPGA sends CLKH when recording starts. The historical four-lane firmware instead sent CLKH all the time, and ran its SPI engine and its two-cycle reset pulses on the returned clock (CLK32MHZ), which the ASIC produces only while CLKH runs. A Frontend design ported from that firmware would have no SPI clock before CLKH starts. If the relayed order is strict, stimulation tables cannot be reloaded during recording without stopping CLKH.
findings.where: Frontend firmware: the SPI engine for 8 DL/DR pairs, BOARD1/3_SPI_CLK and the V6 top SPI clocks, CHIP_RESET (C9) and FE_RESET (D8). CLKH on BOARD1_CLK (G16) and BOARD3_CLK (V17); the eight returned clocks.
findings.evidence: inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md line 67: order is SPI, then resets, then start recording clock. inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/logic_primary_extraction.json slide 13: the FPGA sends 'CLK32MHz_In' to start the recording. inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/rtl_primary_findings.md: the four-lane top connects the SPI engine to the returned clock (top_4lane_framed.v:269-277), reset pulses are two returned-clock cycles, and every historical top drives CLKH continuously (16 MHz).
findings.source: inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/ASIC_REFERENCE.md section 4 and item U05; inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/rtl_primary_findings.md; inputs/asic/ASIC_Reference/logic_primary_extraction.json (slide 13).
findings.consequence: Either the chips cannot be configured before recording starts, or the relayed order is not followed. Experiments that change tables during recording may need recording gaps.
findings.suggested_action: Clock the Frontend SPI engine and reset pulses from the 32 MHz cable clock or Y2, not from a returned clock. Ask the ASIC designer whether SPI loading and resets need CLKH stopped, and whether tables may be reloaded while recording.
findings.corrected: The relayed start-up order loads SPI before CLKH starts, but every historical FPGA top drove CLKH continuously, so that order has never been run. The four-lane top, the only one with a programmable SPI engine, clocks that engine and its command reset pulses from the returned clock, which probably exists only while CLKH runs; the earlier known-good tops clocked their fixed SPI initializer from the local 16 MHz clock, and no recorded test covers SPI loading.
findings.upd_note: This was asked at the meeting of 12 Nov 2026. The ASIC designer said control and start-up behaviour should not matter much at this point, which does not say whether CLKH must be stopped while SPI is loaded or whether tables may be reloaded during recording.

findings.title: On the FPGA-LDO underside port the near board mates through its J4 plug, not its J3, so the "top" board hangs lowest and its J3 receptacle is the open end.
findings.what: FPGA-LDO A J4 and router J4 are DF40C-80DS receptacles on the bottom face, so the board under them must offer a plug: the near board hangs face up and mates with its J4, and the far board mates its J4 into the near board's J3. This works electrically because both V3 boards pass all 80 pins from J3 to J4. But the round-2 description (near board plugs in with its J3; the far board's J4 has nothing above it) holds only for the top-side port. On the underside port the far ("Top") board is the lowest board in the stack, its J4 must be fitted and its J3 receptacle is the exposed end; on the top-side port its J4 plug is the exposed end. Both free ends carry +10 V and -10 V on pins 36/54.
findings.where: FPGA-LDO A and router: J3 DF40C-80DP top, J4 DF40C-80DS bottom, both at (99.783, 113.51). V3 boards: J3 DS on B.Cu, J4 DP on F.Cu. Option A levels (z = 0 at LDO A bottom): near -3.10 to -1.50, far -6.20 to -4.60 on the underside port.
findings.evidence: exports/ldo_a/parts.csv and exports/ldo_b_router/parts.csv (connector types and sides); V3 dumps; ASIC J4 to LDO A / router J4 fit 180 deg, 0.185 mm, pin n on pin n (W/a review working file (not published)); W/a review working file (not published)

findings.suggested_action: Use near/far, not bottom/top, in assembly and firmware notes; fit both connectors on the far board, or make one variant per port; choose a cover for the exposed plug or receptacle.

findings.closed_by: Fixed in pin file V3: all 88 ASIC-to-FPGA inputs (8 data, READ, SYNC and the returned clock of each of the eight chips) have PULLDOWN, so a missing or unpowered ASIC board reads as steady low once the FPGA is configured. The boards carry no resistors on these lines, as before. The check of each returned clock's frequency is so far only a reminder line in the pin file, since no firmware exists yet, and the pin file has not been run in Vivado.

findings.title: Each stack has four stimulation SPI data pairs for eight ASICs, so paired near and far chips get one stream.
findings.closed_by: Closed in V3: SYS-04 is closed as superseded by A-P (blocker). It was closed by the owner's 11 Nov decision and ASIC V4, not by any system CAD fix: in V4 every chip has its own SPI_DINR/SPI_DINL, and the far pair has its own SPI_CLK/SPI_LATCH (J3/J4 pins 66/68/16/18/72/70). On today's Frontend V46, FPGA-LDO A V12 and router V2, those six pins per port reach existing FPGA balls assigned to ASIC outputs (J4 port: T7/R5/C18/D18/P4/P3; J3 port: M2/M4/T15/R13/N3/N4), so the far chips cannot be configured until the pin map V6 file makes them 12 FPGA outputs per stack. SYS-04's 8-line fix must not be built: pins 2/4/6/8/24/58 (its plan used 58/8/24/6) are far-chip READ/DATA outputs in V4 and are unrouted on both FPGA-LDO designs. As a result only 26 of 44 chip outputs per port reach their own FPGA ball; A-P's 12 new routes and new pin file cover this.

findings.title: Ten ASIC-board pass-through vias are open holes inside or at the edge of DF40 pads, so solder can wick away.
findings.closed_by: Closed in V3: Closed by ASIC boards V4: every via whose hole or ring touches a J3/J4 DF40 pad is set filled and capped. That is 62 vias on the top board (18 J3 only, 29 J3+J4, 15 J4 only) and 45 on the bottom board (34 J3+J4, 11 J4 only), all 0.15/0.25 mm F.Cu-B.Cu. The pass-through lanes that had no track now have B.Cu stubs, and the closest open via (bottom board, DISC_OUT(2), ring 0.06 mm from J4-3) is tented. The remaining risk sits in A-4: the fabricator must accept filled-and-capped 0.15 mm via-in-pad (10.7:1 at 1.6 mm), and the order must say so. KiCad's normal Excellon drill set carries no fill data; only the Gerber-format filling/capping drill files (100 top / 83 bottom holes) or IPC-2581 do.
